title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
authors: Riccardo Molteni, Minjun Jeon, Paolo Braccia, Abhinav Deshpande, Vedran Dunjko, Liang Jiang, Su-un Lee, Swarnadeep Majumder, Javier Robledo Moreno, Parthasarathy Suryanarayanan, Kunal Sharma
abstract: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.
summary: This paper introduces Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings, a supervised learning framework that maps classical data into a single, trainable quantum Hamiltonian. By optimizing this Hamiltonian's ground state, the model performs classification, offering theoretical guarantees and demonstrating computational advantages over classical algorithms. It establishes a practical path for implementing QML on near-term quantum hardware.
main_problem: Developing a general quantum machine learning model that is efficiently trainable, provides generalization guarantees, and exhibits computational advantages over classical methods.
main_result: The proposed framework, Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings, successfully establishes a new, theoretically grounded paradigm for QML, demonstrating both its potential for realizing classically hard functions and its scalability on current quantum hardware.
method: The framework encodes a classical dataset into a single, parameterized effective Hamiltonian, whose ground state defines the classification rule. Training involves optimizing the Hamiltonian parameters by minimizing the ground-state energy.
model_or_system: The model operates on an n-qubit Hilbert space, using a data-dependent Hamiltonian $H_T(\alpha)$ derived from encoding unitaries $U(x, \alpha)$ and label operators $O(y)$. Inference is performed by approximating the ground state of this learned Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Test accuracy, ground-state energy, and the ability to realize hypothesis functions beyond classical reach.
important_parameters: Number of qubits ($n$), regularization strength ($\lambda$), and the number of Pauli terms retained after Hamiltonian pruning ($n_P$).
main_assumptions: The realization of classically hard problems relies on standard cryptographic assumptions; gradient estimation relies on the ability to compute expectation values classically.
figures_summary: Figures compare the test accuracy of the Hamiltonian Embedding model against classical solvers and other methods on quantum hardware, showing performance advantages. Other figures compare the required training set size ($L_{90}$) to reach 90% test accuracy.
paper_structure: The paper details the model construction, establishes theoretical properties including generalization bounds and classical surrogates, and concludes with experimental demonstrations on quantum hardware.
why_interesting: The focus on learning structure through Hamiltonian optimization provides a physical, variational approach to QML, which is highly relevant for researchers working on quantum simulation and characterizing complex quantum states.
